content: Photophobia, also referred to as light sensitivity, is a condition characterized by an abnormal sensitivity to light, leading to discomfort or pain in the eyes when exposed to light. It is not a fear of light in the psychological sense but rather a physiological response to light exposure. Photophobia occurs when excessive light enters the eye, overstimulating the photoreceptors in the retina. This overstimulation generates excessive electrical impulses that travel along the optic nerve, resulting in discomfort or pain. Reflexive aversion to light is a common response. Conditions such as corneal abrasions, retinal damage, or impaired pupil constriction (e.g., due to oculomotor nerve damage) can exacerbate this sensitivity by allowing more light to enter the eye than normal. Photophobia can arise from a variety of medical conditions affecting the eyes or the nervous system. These include, but are not limited to: Albinism, which reduces pigmentation in the eyes and increases light sensitivity. The use of anticholinergic drugs, which can paralyze the iris sphincter muscle, preventing proper pupil constriction. Aphakia, the absence of the lens in the eye. Eye burns or injuries. Cataracts, which cloud the lens and alter light transmission. Chiari malformation, a structural defect in the brain affecting the cerebellum. Viral infections such as chikungunya. Conjunctivitis, an inflammation of the conjunctiva. Corneal abrasions or ulcers, which damage the corneal surface. Cystinosis, a metabolic disorder that can affect the eyes. Certain medications, including atropine, cyclopentolate, and others, which may induce photophobia as a side effect. Neurological conditions such as encephalitis or meningitis. Eye diseases or infections, such as chalazion, episcleritis, glaucoma, or keratoconus. Hangovers, which can temporarily increase light sensitivity. Idiopathic anterior uveitis or iritis, which involve inflammation of the uvea or iris. Influenza, which can cause systemic symptoms including photophobia. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye syndrome). Lightly pigmented eyes, which may be more sensitive to light. Migraines, which are often accompanied by photophobia. Mydriatic drug use, which dilates the pupils and increases light entry. Retinal detachment, a serious condition where the retina separates from its underlying tissue. Subarachnoid hemorrhage, a type of brain bleed that can cause neurological symptoms, including photophobia. Patients with photophobia often avoid direct light exposure, such as sunlight or bright indoor lighting. They may seek refuge in dark rooms or wear sunglasses to reduce discomfort. Common symptoms associated with photophobia include: Eye pain. Headache. Nausea. Neck stiffness. Blurred vision. Eye soreness or wounds. Redness of the eyes. Itching or swelling of the eyes. Dizziness. Numbness or tingling sensations in other parts of the body. Changes in hearing. Interestingly, photophobia is not limited to humans. Certain insects and animals also exhibit photophobic behavior, actively avoiding light to protect themselves.
